title: How Developing Countries Can Do More With Less
gist: As foreign-aid cuts squeeze African development budgets, three authors argue that development evaluation frameworks have long been shaped by donor priorities rather than local communities, and that this moment of scarcity is an opportunity to adopt 'Made in Africa Evaluation' approaches that treat local knowledge as valid evidence, arguing that without control over evaluation and evidence itself, calls to 'decolonize development' remain hollow.

themes.theme: Evaluation as a political, not neutral, exercise

insights.claim: Development evaluation is often presented as a neutral technical exercise measuring whether projects met their objectives, but it is actually deeply political because it determines what is seen as important, whose knowledge is trusted, which programs keep receiving funding, and ultimately how resources are allocated.
insights.speaker: Takunda Chirau
insights.so_what: Reframes M&E (monitoring and evaluation) methodology choice as a lever of power over aid allocation, not a back-office technical detail -- relevant to any institution designing or funding evaluation systems.
insights.quote: evaluation is deeply political: it reflects what is seen as important and whose knowledge is trusted, and it influences which programs continue to receive funding
insights.locator: The answer lies in how development is monitored and evaluated

insights.claim: Evaluation frameworks have historically been shaped by donor priorities aimed at tracking and comparing results across contexts, causing them to fail to capture local realities and treat affected communities as sources of data rather than partners in defining what meaningful change looks like.
insights.speaker: Takunda Chirau
insights.so_what: Donor-designed universal metrics may systematically misjudge program success/failure in local terms, a risk for any investor or funder relying on standard donor evaluation reports to judge program effectiveness.
insights.quote: donors' expectations and desired outputs take precedence over those of local communities
insights.locator: To date, evaluation frameworks have largely been influenced by donor priorities

themes.theme: Made in Africa Evaluation as an alternative model

insights.claim: The 'Made in Africa Evaluation' approach seeks to assess development projects according to African realities, values, and priorities by recognizing Indigenous knowledge, local institutions, and community experience as legitimate sources of evidence, shifting who holds authority over knowledge production.
insights.speaker: Takunda Chirau
insights.so_what: A named, adoptable evaluation methodology that African governments, regional bodies, or aid recipients could formally institutionalize as aid volumes decline and accountability demands rise.
insights.locator: African countries and communities, in particular, could adopt Made in Africa Evaluation approaches

insights.claim: When rural health committees monitor clinic performance using community-designed scorecards rather than relying on donor audits, facility managers can identify and respond more quickly to drug shortages, long wait times, or service gaps.
insights.speaker: Takunda Chirau
insights.so_what: A concrete mechanism (community scorecards) shown to produce faster operational fixes than donor audits -- a model transferable to other service-delivery monitoring contexts.
insights.locator: when rural health committees monitor clinic performance

insights.claim: When farmers help assess irrigation projects, evaluations have revealed practical constraints -- unreliable water supplies, inadequate maintenance, and inequitable land distribution -- that externally designed indicators tend to overlook.
insights.speaker: Takunda Chirau
insights.so_what: Illustrates concrete blind spots (water reliability, maintenance, land equity) that top-down evaluation metrics miss in agricultural development projects -- relevant for anyone assessing irrigation/agriculture project impact reports.
insights.locator: Similarly, when farmers help assess irrigation projects

themes.theme: Beyond representation: control over evidence itself

insights.claim: The African Union and its member states have long called for reforms to international development and financial architecture -- greater representation, more equitable financing, a stronger voice in global decision-making -- but these reform efforts often overlook a more powerful driver of change: control over knowledge and evidence production.
insights.speaker: Takunda Chirau
insights.so_what: Argues that governance-seat reforms are insufficient without control over the evaluation/evidence apparatus itself -- a structural critique relevant to debates on IMF/World Bank/MDB voting-share reform.
insights.locator: But these reforms, while important, often overlook another powerful driver of change

insights.claim: Without significant changes to evaluation practices and the resulting knowledge production, calls to 'decolonize development' will continue to ring hollow.
insights.speaker: Takunda Chirau
insights.so_what: Sets a concrete bar for judging whether 'decolonization' rhetoric in development institutions is substantive: has control over evaluation/evidence actually shifted, not just governance seats.
insights.quote: Without significant changes to evaluation and the resulting knowledge production, calls to "decolonize development" will continue to ring hollow.
insights.locator: Structural transformation requires giving them a greater role
